passage:
Dear Shreya,

Thanks for not laughing when I told you about last week. My cousin's wedding meant four nights of bed at three and up at noon, and by Sunday my routine was gone. I sat there feeling as if I'd ruined a whole month of work. Then I remembered what you said: one slip is not a verdict. So on Monday I did only one thing: alarm at seven, curtains open, breakfast. No punishment, no marathon revision. On Tuesday I was tired. By Wednesday I was nearly back, and bedtime came on its own. I keep the wake time fixed and treat the rest as adjustable. Want to walk before school on Thursday?

Harsha

qa.q: How many nights did the wedding shift Harsha's sleep?
qa.a: The wedding meant four nights of bed at three and up at noon.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel on Sunday, and what changed?
qa.a: Harsha felt as if a month of work was ruined, but remembering that one slip is not a verdict made it possible to restart.

qa.q: What else could Harsha do to protect the routine before the next big event, and why?
qa.a: Harsha could keep the wake time as close as possible during the event and plan an easy morning the day after, because a quick restart is easier when the anchor is kept.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Shreya probably feels glad and useful, since the earlier advice helped Harsha to restart. 🙂

grounding: After a week of late nights around a wedding, the student does not give up but returns to the fixed wake time the next morning, treating the slip as normal rather than proof of failure.

passage:
So, Kavitha, you asked how I didn't lose my routine after my cousin's wedding week? Honestly, I did lose it. That's the story.

I'm Jaya. Before the wedding, I'd been waking at 6:30 every day for a month. Then the wedding came. Sangeet till 2 am, mehendi, haldi, relatives in every room, and one night I slept at 4. For a whole week I barely saw a morning.

The day after the wedding, I woke up at noon, looked at my chart with all its ticks, and thought, great, I've ruined everything. I almost tore it down.

But then I thought, one bad week isn't the whole month. It's just a week. So the very next morning I set the alarm for 6:30 again. I was a zombie that day. But I got up.

Within four days I was back. Slipping isn't failing. Stopping is.

qa.q: What time did Jaya set the alarm for the morning after the wedding?
How did Jaya feel on waking at noon after the wedding?
qa.a: Jaya felt discouraged and frustrated, thinking everything was ruined and nearly tearing the chart down.

qa.q: What could Jaya plan before the next festival or wedding?
qa.a: Jaya could decide in advance to go straight back to 6:30 the morning after it ends, so the return is automatic rather than a debate.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel reassured and less alone, since Jaya admits slipping too and shows that returning quickly is what matters.

grounding: A spoken account of a student whose routine slips during a wedding week, who returns to the fixed wake time next morning and treats the slip as normal.

passage:
I'm Tanvir, Madhuri's neighbour on the third floor, and we walk to the school bus together. For most of the term she was at the gate at 6:50 sharp, hair still wet, eating a banana.

Then Diwali week came. Her building balcony had lights and music every night, and her cousins from Nagpur stayed over. For eight days I waited at the gate alone. Once I saw her through the window at 7:20, still asleep on the sofa.

The Monday after the cousins left, I assumed she'd be late again. But at 6:50 she was there, hair wet, banana in hand, eyes half shut.

"You're back," I said.

She yawned. "It was just a week. It's not the end of the world."

She looked exhausted for a few days. I don't know if she felt guilty about Diwali week. But by Friday she was chatting again at the gate, back to her usual self.

qa.q: What time was Madhuri usually at the gate?
What might Madhuri have been feeling when she said "It was just a week"?
qa.a: She seemed tired but calm and unbothered, treating the slip as normal rather than feeling like a failure, though Tanvir can't be sure.

qa.q: What would you suggest Madhuri keep doing after holidays?
qa.a: Keep returning to the fixed wake time the very next morning, even while tired, since that is what brought her back to normal by Friday.

qa.q: How did Madhuri's comeback look to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir expected her to stay late, so seeing her back at 6:50 on Monday was a surprise, and a sign the routine was stronger than one festival week.

grounding: An observer describes a student whose routine slipped during a festival week and who simply returned to her fixed wake time the next morning.
